title: King's Indian Defence: the locked chain and the two plans
outcomes: Names the chain that arises after 4...d6 5.Nf3 O-O 6.Be2 e5 7.O-O Nc6 8.d5 (White c4, d5 and e4; Black d6 and e5) and the wing each side plays on
Finds White's c5 break when a knight on d3 supports it, and sees that c5 is not automatic when it does not
Finds Black's kingside pawn advance (f5, f4, g5) and carries the plan on when the pawn has reached f4
Checks what the opponent's last move attacks before capturing or pushing a pawn, and recognises a position with no locked chain where neither plan applies

steps.text: **King's Indian Defence**, normal variation (ECO E70): 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.e4 d6. In our sample of online rated games (September 2026, 4,752,291 games, first 16 plies) 14,263 visits reach this position. This lesson follows one main line in which the centre becomes locked, the chain you met in the King's Indian chain lesson (not taught again here), and looks at the two plans that follow: White queenside space with c5; Black kingside play with ...f5.

steps.caption: Position after 4...d6, White to move. Step through one main line. Other moves are possible; this line shows how the chain arises and where each plan starts.

line.say: Nf3 develops the knight; it controls e5 and defends the pawn on d4.
e5 challenges the pawn on d4 and fights for the centre.
Nc6 adds a second attacker on d4.
d5 attacks the knight and locks the centre: White pawns on c4, d5 and e4 face Black pawns on d6 and e5. Now each side plays on its own wing.
Ne7 retreats and gets ready for the pawn move ...f5.
Ne1 heads for d3, where it will support c5.
Nd7 clears the f-pawn's path and heads for c5 or f6.
Be3 develops the bishop and covers c5 and d4.
f5 is Black's break: it attacks the pawn on e4 and starts the kingside plan.

claims.statement: After ...e5 the pawn on e5 attacks d4.
After d5 the white pawn stands on d5.
After d5 the white pawn still stands on e4.
After d5 the black pawn stands on d6.
After d5 the black pawn stands on e5.
After Ne7 the knight guards f5.
After Ne1 the knight can reach d3 and f3.
After ...f5 the pawn on f5 attacks e4.
Both kings are on the kingside: White's after O-O.
Black's king is on the kingside after O-O.
After Be3 the bishop covers c5 and d4.
After Nf3 the knight covers e5 and defends d4.

steps.text: **White's plan: c5 (rule of thumb).** In the locked centre White has more room on the queenside. The break is c5, which attacks the pawn on d6. Condition: the pawn should be supported, here by a knight on d3, and Black's kingside play must not be faster. In the next item, find the move and check what the pawn on c5 attacks.

**Black's plan: f5, f4, g5 (rule of thumb).** Black has more room on the kingside. The break ...f5 challenges e4; ...f4 and ...g5 follow to attack White's king. Condition: the centre must stay locked, and it is a plan, not a guarantee. It is a race, and a tempting capture can cost more than it gains. Masters (329,379 games, both 2500+): after 9.Ne1 Nd7 10.Be3, all 50 games went ...f5; a small sample. Next, the pawn has reached f4.

**Check before you push (rule of thumb).** Your plan tells you which moves to look at; it does not tell you what the opponent's last move attacks or whether a capture works. Here White has just played c5, which attacks the pawn on d6. Black can capture on c5 (dxc5), or take on e4 with the knight. The engine's verdicts on both are shown in the next item. Check what each capture leaves behind, then decide.

steps.title: One move changes whether c5 works
steps.prompt: In all three positions White considers c5, after the same twelve moves by each side. The first two differ only in White's thirteenth move (Nd3 or Kh1). The third differs from the first only in Black's thirteenth move (Rf7 or Ng6). Predict each, then check.
Think about the positions you played without hints. Before you chose a move, what did you check? Write one line for each side.
